paras: The attempted lynching of Simon Raten was a gathering of up to 2,000 people at the city prison in Sacramento, California, on the night of April 11, 1882, who meant to hang Raten, a jailed Siberian-born railroad worker accused of fatally shooting hotel proprietor James Lansing. Police, National Guard companies with a Gatling gun, and an appeal by Mayor John Q. Brown turned the crowd away without violence. Raten was convicted of first-degree murder a month later and sentenced to hang.

According to the Sacramento Daily Record-Union, Raten, a copper worker in the railroad shops, had been beaten by fellow worker Andrew Erickson in a quarrel on Sunday, April 9. About 4:30 p.m. the next day he was accused of firing at Erickson on K street, missing him and wounding John J. Livingston in the hand. Pursued by a crowd into the alley behind the International Hotel, he was said to have shot Lansing, who had stepped out of his yard and cried "Don't shoot." As officers forced the captured man into a hack, a crowd on Third street shouted "Hang him!" and "Kill him!"

Lansing, a former city marshal, sheriff and county assessor, died at 5 p.m. on April 11, and the tolling of the fire bells drew hundreds to his hotel. The Record-Union wrote that men there openly declared that "a little wholesome hanging" was needed. By about 9 p.m. some 1,200 men and boys had gathered at the city prison, a number that grew to 2,000, though the paper saw no leader among them.

Chief of Police Karcher obtained an order from Governor Perkins, and Colonel T. W. Sheehan marched Companies A and G and a platoon of Company B from a drill to the prison, later bringing up a Gatling gun. Members of the crowd jeered the troops, and the paper judged that it showed a disposition to hang Raten to the nearest lamp-post, though many had come out of curiosity. Mayor Brown then spoke from an improvised rostrum, promised a speedy trial and led part of the crowd away, and by 11 p.m. few people remained.

The Record-Union reported that citizens had met that night to consider a raid on the jail, and rumors of Vigilantes circulated, though these could not be confirmed. Raten was examined on April 12, held for murder without bail and moved to the County Jail, where twenty militiamen and a Gatling gun guarded him at night. A coroner's inquest heard witnesses to the shooting the same evening.

His trial opened May 10, and on May 12 a jury found him guilty of murder in the first degree. He was sentenced to hang on July 26, 1882, after a statement in court accusing city officers, and in December his appeal was set for hearing before the state Supreme Court. No report of the appeal's outcome or of an execution was found.

The local Record-Union carried the fullest coverage, calling Raten "A Murderous Tartar" and "the assassin" and describing the crowd as representing "the best citizens." The same paper credited the police and militia with averting "the disgrace of a lynching in the capital city of the State," while writing that a promised speedy trial would do most to calm the public. Its later editorial praised the conviction within a month and two days as a rebuke to insanity pleas.

Out of town, the Los Angeles Herald and the Arizona Weekly Citizen ran a Sacramento dispatch under the heading "A Mob Gathers" or as plain telegraph news, and the Washington Evening Star reduced the night to an "unsuccessful attempt" to lynch "Simon Baton." Nevada papers followed the case, the Eureka Sentinel calling Raten "a Russian" and the Carson Morning Appeal welcoming the verdict.

The Evening Star called the episode an attempted lynching, but the local account says the crowd made no move on the prison before the troops arrived. Alexander Rothenstein told the Record-Union that Raten's real name was "Simanoff" and that he had a criminal past, claims Raten partly denied.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Simon Raten
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A crowd of 1,200 to 2,000 gathered at the Sacramento city prison intending to hang a jailed man accused of murder and was turned back by police, militia and the mayor (A2, A3, A4); the accused was a Siberian-born man, not Black (A1, A2, A14).
No one was killed: the crowd that gathered to hang Raten for the shooting of James Lansing dispersed without taking him, and he was later tried and sentenced in court (A2, A11, A15).

The local Record-Union (A2, A3) and a separate Sacramento wire dispatch (A4, reprinted in A8) agree on the crowd at the jail, the National Guard and the dispersal, and a Washington telegram (A5) reports the failed attempt.

accounts.label: Sacramento Record-Union (local)
accounts.gist: Several thousand gathered at the prison after Lansing's death and spoke of a 'wholesome hanging', but no demonstration was made before the militia arrived, and the crowd dispersed after the mayor's speech.

accounts.label: Sacramento wire dispatch
accounts.gist: A crowd surrounded Lansing's hotel and went to the jail; fearing a lynching, police called four National Guard companies, and the crowd slowly dispersed after the mayor spoke.

accounts.label: Washington telegram
accounts.gist: Described the night as an 'unsuccessful attempt' to lynch 'Simon Baton'.

framing.detail: The Record-Union headlined Raten as 'A Murderous Tartar' and 'the assassin', described the crowd as 'the best citizens' with community sympathy, yet praised officers for averting 'the disgrace of a lynching' and urged a speedy trial.
Out-of-town papers ran the Sacramento dispatch under 'A Mob Gathers' or a one-line telegram.
After the verdict the Record-Union and the Carson Morning Appeal praised the quick conviction and anticipated execution.
